name: Globe and Mail cryptic crossword No 3,361

clue.text: Some go on about Rikki-Tikki-Tavi? (8)

indicators.note: 'about' here means roughly, approximately — and letters given only approximately are letters free to come out in another order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eight letters

annotation.surface: A few people will not stop talking about a character out of Kipling.
annotation.walkthrough: Rikki-Tikki-Tavi is the snake-killing hero of Kipling's Jungle Book story, and the question mark marks him as one example of his species rather than a synonym for it.
annotation.definitionFit: Rikki-Tikki-Tavi is Kipling's mongoose, so the name defines the animal by example, which is what the question mark admits.

clue.text: Given wrong role in new production of Cats after endless failure (7)

indicators.note: a new production stages the same material afresh, so the letters of the title beside it are restaged in a different order
'after' means later, so the restaged four letters take the back of the answer and the piece they follow takes the front
'endless' takes the end off the word it governs, leaving it one letter short

blocks.note: a failure is a MISS, docked of its final letter
the four letters of CATS restaged in another order

annotation.surface: An unlucky actor lands the wrong part in a revival of Cats.
annotation.walkthrough: Cats is italicised in the paper because it is the musical, so the whole clue passes as theatre gossip. The failure being shortened is a MISS, not the flop the surface offers.
annotation.definitionFit: To miscast is exactly to give a performer the wrong role, and both definition and answer are past participles.

clue.text: Shark in harbour (5)

blocks.note: dictionaries list this word as a shark in its own right — the slow, docile bottom-feeder of warm coastal seas
to harbour a grudge is to keep it warm and alive rather than let it go, which is what this verb does to a grievance

annotation.surface: A shark has come into the harbour.
annotation.walkthrough: Both halves are definitions with nothing to assemble, and the trap is reading 'in harbour' as where the shark is. The nurse shark is a real species, not a joke about hospitals.
annotation.definitionFit: A nurse is a shark, the docile bottom-feeder divers swim beside, and to nurse a grudge is to harbour it.

clue.text: Cry after falling over, say, so paid off (4,1,5)

indicators.note: something off is not as it should be — off-key, off-form — so the letters beside it are out of their proper order

blocks.note: o is the cricket scorecard's short form for an over
anagram fodder, nine letters, joining the o already found

annotation.surface: A yelp after a tumble, and a debt settled into the bargain.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Over' belongs to 'falling over' on the surface and is the cricketer's single letter underneath. The answer is what an adult says while picking a toddler back up.
annotation.definitionFit: Oops-a-daisy is the noise you let out, or make on a child's behalf, in the second after a tumble.

clue.text: Convert seen with leader of zealots at end of the blessed event? (6)

indicators.note: to convert a thing is to turn it into something else, and letters converted come out in a different order
the leader of a word is the letter standing at its front
what is at the end of a word is its final letter

blocks.note: anagram fodder, four letters
the leading letter of Zealots
the last letter of thE

annotation.surface: A convert turns up with the head zealot at the close of a joyful occasion.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Blessed event' normally announces a baby; here it is the thing that earns a 'bless you' from everyone in the room. 'Convert' opens the clue looking like a noun and is the instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: A sneeze is the event that draws 'bless you', so the phrase that usually means a birth is borrowed as a joke, flagged by the question mark.

clue.text: Finishing touch of chives with Kitty’s pea soup? (4)

indicators.note: the finishing touch is the last thing added, so it asks for the final letter of the word that follows

blocks.note: the last letter of chiveS
a mog, or moggy, is the British word for an ordinary cat; the ’s reads as 'is' in the surface

annotation.surface: A bowl of pea soup finished with chives, served up by Kitty.
annotation.walkthrough: A pea-souper was the thick yellow London fog of the coal-fire era, dense enough to lose a bus in, and that is the sense the question mark points at.
annotation.definitionFit: Pea soup, or a pea-souper, is the old name for air too thick and yellow to see through, which is what smog is.

clue.text: Topless American in tiny swimsuit (7)

indicators.note: topless means without its top, and the top of a word in a down clue is the letter at its head
'in' puts what stands before it inside what stands after it

blocks.note: a mini is anything tiny — the skirt, the car, the break
an American is a YANK, beheaded of its Y

annotation.surface: An American with no top on, poured into a very small swimsuit.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Topless' does the deletion and the leering at once. The mankini is the lime-green sling Sacha Baron Cohen's Borat wore in 2006, after which it became a British stag-night standby.
annotation.definitionFit: A mankini is a swimsuit, the man's sling-shaped one-piece, so the definition names it by plain category.

clue.text: Complaint from adult overheard (5)

indicators.note: overheard means caught by ear, so the word beside it is to be taken by its sound and not its spelling

blocks.note: an adult is grown, and grown is the word you hear

annotation.surface: Somebody catches a grown-up grumbling.
annotation.walkthrough: Four words do three jobs here: definition, sound source, homophone signal. 'Adult' looks like the person doing the complaining and is really the word to say out loud.
annotation.definitionFit: A groan is a complaint made aloud without words, the noise of somebody who has had enough.

clue.text: Saint criticised and beaten (8)

blocks.note: the standard abbreviation, as in St Paul's
to rap somebody is to criticise them sharply — a rap on the knuckles

annotation.surface: A saint who was criticised and then beaten.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Beaten' means thrashed with a strap rather than defeated, which is the sense the martyrdom surface quietly supports. ST for saint is the first abbreviation any solver meets.
annotation.definitionFit: Strapped means beaten with a strap, the old schoolroom punishment, so the past participle answers the definition directly.

clue.text: Digging through Latin tomes (4)

definitions.note: 'Digging' is a verb in its slang sense of being keen on something, while the answer is a preposition; the two swap freely all the same, since digging jazz and being into jazz say the same thing.

indicators.note: something that runs through a phrase passes straight across it, so the letters lie consecutively in the words that follow

blocks.note: four consecutive letters, starting in the middle of the first word and finishing at the start of the second

annotation.surface: A scholar burrowing through heavy volumes of Latin.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a researcher at work and 'digging' is the hipster's verb for being keen. A run of letters that crosses a word boundary hides better than one sitting in a single word.
annotation.definitionFit: Being into something and digging it are the same enthusiasm, a slang sense the two words have shared since the 1950s.

clue.text: Show it’s all true somehow (10)

indicators.note: by some unspecified means — so the letters reach the answer in an order nobody has specified

blocks.note: anagram fodder, ten letters

annotation.surface: Insisting the story really is true, one way or another.
annotation.walkthrough: A ten-letter answer with a one-word definition is the classic shape of an anagram. The apostrophe in it's simply vanishes — punctuation never counts as a letter.
annotation.definitionFit: To illustrate a point is to show it, to make it visible by example, so the two verbs swap directly.

clue.text: Where gladiators battled a long time back (5)

indicators.note: back sends the letters the other way, and in an across entry that means reading them right to left

blocks.note: a long time is an era, and the clue's 'a' supplies the article in front of it

annotation.surface: Remembering the place gladiators fought, a long while ago.
annotation.walkthrough: 'A long time back' reads as one phrase meaning ages ago, so the 'back' has to be prised off it to work as the turn instruction. The article travels with its noun.
annotation.definitionFit: The arena was the sanded floor of the Roman amphitheatre, the ground gladiators fought on, so the definition places it exactly.

clue.text: Countless multitude sick in Holy City (7)

indicators.note: 'in' places what stands before it inside what stands after it

blocks.note: Zion is the hill of Jerusalem and, in scripture and hymns, a name for the holy city itself
ill = sick

annotation.surface: A vast crowd falling ill in Jerusalem.
annotation.walkthrough: Zion stands for the whole of Jerusalem wherever hymns and psalms are sung, which is what makes 'Holy City' fair for it. The definition is two words doing one job.
annotation.definitionFit: A zillion is the comic word for a number too large to bother counting, so it names a countless multitude.

clue.text: Nearly reach a new tropical bird (6)

indicators.note: nearly means not quite all the way, so the word it governs stops one letter short of its end

blocks.note: to reach is to TOUCH, stopped one letter short
used literally
n is the standard short form for new

annotation.surface: Almost getting to a newly arrived tropical bird.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Reach' is the verb meaning to touch, not to arrive at, and that swap is the only hard step. Guinness posters made the toucan Britain's default tropical bird.
annotation.definitionFit: A toucan is the South American bird with the enormous coloured bill, tropical by any reckoning.

clue.text: Churn nun made lacking a handle (7)

indicators.note: to churn is to agitate something until everything in it has shifted position, which is what happens to the letters beside it

blocks.note: anagram fodder, seven letters

annotation.surface: A butter churn a nun made, with no handle on it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Handle' is slang for the name somebody goes by, and that sense carries the whole definition while the surface offers the thing you grip on a churn.
annotation.definitionFit: A handle is a person's name in slang, so whatever lacks a handle has no name to be called by.

clue.text: Fine wordplay — sort of (6)

blocks.note: a pun is the commonest kind of wordplay there is
-ish on the end of a word means roughly, sort of: sixish, greenish

annotation.surface: Some rather good wordplay, more or less.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Fine' is the verb — what a magistrate does to you — and it opens the clue looking like praise for the wordplay that follows. Ish now stands on its own in speech.
annotation.definitionFit: Fining somebody is one way of punishing them, so the narrower verb stands in for the wider one.

clue.text: Character popular on social media cheats at hard game for children (7)

blocks.note: to have somebody is to cheat them — you've been had
h is the pencil-grading short form for hard
tag is the playground chasing game

annotation.surface: Somebody well known online cheats at a hard children's game.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cheats at hard' splits where the surface does not want it to. The cheating verb is have, as in you've been had, and hard is the H stamped on a pencil.
annotation.definitionFit: A hashtag is the # character that social media runs on, which is what the definition describes.

clue.text: Buffet food may be fried in this (6)

definitions.text: food may be fried in this

blocks.note: to buffet is to strike again and again, what wind and waves do to a coastline

blocks.clueFragment: food may be fried in this
blocks.note: the flour-and-egg mixture a chip shop dips everything in before it goes in the fryer

annotation.surface: A buffet at which the food may have been fried.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Buffet' is the verb that rhymes with tuft it, not the French noun with the sandwiches, and the mention of food keeps the wrong pronunciation alive to the end.
annotation.definitionFit: To buffet is to batter, to strike repeatedly; and batter is also the flour-and-egg coating fish is fried in.

clue.text: Players checking an answer in game (7)

indicators.note: to check a thing is to hold it in and arrest its movement, so the word doing the checking closes round what it holds

blocks.note: the cast is the company of players in a production
used literally, held after the first letter of the company
a is the standard short form for answer, as in Q and A

annotation.surface: A team checking over an answer in the middle of a game.
annotation.walkthrough: 'An answer' looks like one phrase and is two separate pieces: the article gets held inside the players, and the single letter waits outside on the end.
annotation.definitionFit: Canasta is the rummy-style card game that swept Britain and America in the 1950s, so 'game' names it by category.

clue.text: Community cut part of canal (5)

indicators.note: a thing cut is shortened, and a word cut loses the letter standing at its end

blocks.note: a colony is a community of settlers living together

annotation.surface: A community cut off, beside part of a canal.
annotation.walkthrough: The canal is the alimentary one that runs through you, not the waterway the surface is digging. A colony is the community being shortened.
annotation.definitionFit: The colon is the large intestine, a stretch of the alimentary canal, so the definition places the answer anatomically.

clue.text: Secures government charge for auditor (5)

indicators.note: an auditor is one who listens, so the words are offered for the ear and their spelling is not to be trusted

blocks.note: the charge a government levies is a tax, and that is the sound to write down

annotation.surface: The government levies a charge, and the auditor looks it over.
annotation.walkthrough: An auditor audits accounts on the surface and listens underneath — the same Latin root serves both. 'Secures' is the definition: to tack something down.
annotation.definitionFit: To tack something is to fasten it with tacks, so the definition matches the answer as a verb and in number.

clue.text: I start to gag surrounded by vehicle’s smoke (5)

indicators.note: the start of a word is the letter it opens with
what is surrounded sits inside, so the word named after it closes round the letters before it

blocks.note: a car is the everyday vehicle; the ’s reads as 'is' in the surface
used literally
the first letter of Gag

annotation.surface: The speaker begins to retch, hemmed in by the fug inside a car.
annotation.walkthrough: The I is doing literal duty, which is easy to miss in a clue that reads as a first-person complaint. 'Smoke' is the noun — the thing you light, not what comes off it.
annotation.definitionFit: A smoke is something you smoke, the cigar you step outside for, a casual noun sense the answer fits exactly.

clue.text: Climbers clutching tree branch (4)

indicators.note: what is clutched is held tight inside the grip, so the letters sit inside the word doing the clutching

blocks.note: four consecutive letters sit inside this single word, starting after its first

annotation.surface: Climbers grabbing hold of a branch.
annotation.walkthrough: A hidden run inside one word is harder to spot than one spanning a gap, because there is no join to catch the eye. A limb of a tree is a main bough, not a twig.
annotation.definitionFit: A limb of a tree is one of its main branches, a sense as old as the one covering arms and legs.

clue.text: Uncurved narrow passageway in ear (8)

indicators.note: what arrives in the ear is a sound, so the words before it are to be heard rather than read

blocks.note: a narrow passage of water between two land masses is a strait, and that is what you say aloud

annotation.surface: A narrow, uncurved channel running into the ear.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue also reads as anatomy, since the ear has canals of its own, which is how 'in ear' passes as scenery rather than an instruction. A strait is the sea passage at Dover or Gibraltar.
annotation.definitionFit: Straight means not bent or curved, the plainest adjective sense of the word.

clue.text: Lacking clothes and undies periodically (4)

indicators.note: what happens periodically happens at regular intervals, so letters are taken at a fixed spacing instead of all together

blocks.note: every second letter across the two words, beginning with the second

annotation.surface: Somebody with no clothes on, and only occasional underwear.
annotation.walkthrough: 'And' is pulling its weight rather than joining — the run of letters starts inside it. Periodically is the gentler cousin of 'oddly' and 'evenly'.
annotation.definitionFit: Nude means wearing nothing at all, so lacking clothes describes the state precisely.

clue.text: Customer at last got free new jumper (4,4)

indicators.note: 'at last' points to the end of the word before it, which is its final letter
something new is made afresh out of the same material, so the letters are rebuilt in a different order

blocks.note: the last letter of customeR
anagram fodder, seven letters

annotation.surface: A customer finally got a new jumper for nothing.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Jumper' is the creature that jumps, not the woollen thing going over the counter, and in a British paper the woollen one comes to mind first.
annotation.definitionFit: A tree frog jumps from branch to branch, so 'jumper' defines it by what it does rather than by what it is.
